chapter.name: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet

questions.q: Fig. 13.1 of the chapter names five layers of Earth: crust, upper mantle, lower mantle, outer core and inner core. In which of these layers does all life on Earth exist?
questions.a: The crust
o: The crust
The upper mantle
The outer core
The lower mantle

questions.q: Table 13.1 lists this as an interesting feature of Earth: 'We can stand on the ground held by gravity, but our heart can pump blood up to our head.' Why does the chapter find this interesting?
questions.a: Gravity pulls everything towards the ground, blood included, yet the heart can still push blood upward to the head
o: Gravity pulls everything towards the ground, blood included, yet the heart can still push blood upward to the head
Gravity acts only on solid things like our bodies, not on liquids like blood, so blood rises to the head on its own
Blood, like the air we breathe, has no fixed volume, so it spreads up to the head without any push
Gravity holds only our feet to the ground; the blood inside the body feels no pull at all

questions.q:
Match each layer of Earth named in Fig. 13.1 (Column I) with where it lies (Column II).
Column I: 1. Crust, 2. Upper mantle, 3. Lower mantle, 4. Outer core
Column II: A. Between the upper mantle and the outer core, B. Between the lower mantle and the inner core, C. The outermost layer of Earth, D. Between the crust and the lower mantle

Assertion (A): Earth is the only planet known where life, as we know it today, exists and thrives in all its forms.
Reason (R): Earth is a planet that orbits the Sun.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or false? 'Table 13.1 finds it interesting that the air we breathe does not fly off into space, because gases have a fixed volume and their particles stay in one place.' Give a reason or write the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter recalls from Chapter 7 that the particles of a gas move freely and gases do not have a fixed volume. That is why it is interesting that the air we breathe does not fly off and disappear into space.
s: States False
Corrects it: gas particles move freely and gases have no fixed volume, so we might expect the air to escape into space

questions.q:
(a) About how many planets does the chapter say there may be in the universe?
(b) On how many of these planets is life, as we know it today, known to exist and thrive?
questions.a: (a) Perhaps billions. (b) Only one: Earth.
s: (a) Perhaps billions
(b) Only one, Earth

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) Like the other planets of the solar system, Earth orbits the Sun. Why, then, does the chapter say that Earth is 'not just any planet'?
(b) Name the two layers that make up Earth's core in Fig. 13.1, and say which of them is at the very centre.
(c) Name one material that the chapter says Earth gives us for building, and say what soil helps us do.
questions.a: (a) Because Earth is a planet that sustains life: it is the only planet known where life, as we know today, exists and thrives in all its forms. (b) The outer core and the inner core; the inner core is at the very centre. (c) Rock or timber, with which we build homes, buildings and roads; soil helps in growing crops.
s: (a) Earth sustains life: it is the only planet known where life exists and thrives
(b) The outer core and the inner core; the inner core is at the centre
(c) Rock or timber for building; soil helps in growing crops

questions.q: Sameer says: 'The deepest ocean trench goes down below the crust, so the animals living at the bottom of the trench must live in the mantle.' Check his claim using what the chapter says about the crust.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. The chapter says that the crust, where all of life exists, stretches from the tallest mountain to the deepest ocean trench. So even the bottom of the deepest trench is still part of the crust, and the animals there live in the crust, not in the mantle. All life on Earth is found in this thin surface layer.
s: States that the claim is wrong
Uses the chapter: the crust runs from the tallest mountain to the deepest ocean trench
Concludes that trench animals live in the crust, since all life is in the crust and none in the mantle

questions.q:
The eco-club of a school in Madurai must choose one caption for a wall display on Section 13.1 of the chapter. Three captions are suggested.
P: 'Earth gives us air, water and soil, but nothing to build our homes with'
Q: 'Air that stays, blood that climbs: everyday wonders of Earth'
R: 'Earth: the only planet in the universe'
(a) What is wrong with caption P?
(b) What is wrong with caption R?
(c) Which caption fits the chapter, and which two features of Earth in Table 13.1 does it point to?
(d) Rewrite caption R so that it agrees with the chapter.
questions.a: (a) P is wrong because the chapter says Earth also provides materials like rock and timber, with which we build our homes, buildings and roads. (b) R is wrong because the chapter says there are perhaps billions of planets in the universe; Earth is only the one known planet where life, as we know it, exists and thrives. (c) Q fits the chapter. It points to the two features in Table 13.1: the air we breathe does not fly off into space, even though gas particles move freely and gases have no fixed volume; and although gravity holds us on the ground, our heart can pump blood up to our head. (d) For example: 'Earth: the only planet known to support life'.
s: (a) P is wrong: Earth also gives rock and timber for building homes, buildings and roads
(b) R is wrong: there are perhaps billions of planets; Earth is the only one known with life
(c) Chooses Q: the air does not fly off into space, and the heart pumps blood up to the head though gravity holds us down
(d) A corrected caption saying Earth is the only planet known to support life

questions.q: Which list gives the four planets nearest the Sun in order of increasing distance from the Sun?
questions.a: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
o: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
Venus, Mercury, Earth, Mars
Mercury, Earth, Venus, Mars
Mercury, Venus, Mars, Earth

questions.q: Astronomers study two rocky planets of another star (an imaginary example). Planet X is farther from the star than Planet Y, yet Planet X has the higher average temperature. Using the chapter's explanation for Venus, what is the most likely reason?
questions.a: Planet X has a thick atmosphere of gases like carbon dioxide that trap heat
o: Planet X has a thick atmosphere of gases like carbon dioxide that trap heat
Planet X has no atmosphere, so the star's heat reaches its surface freely
Planet X is a large planet made mostly of gases
Planet X goes round its star in a nearly circular orbit

questions.q: Table 13.2 records whether Mercury, Venus and Earth have an atmosphere. Going by the chapter's explanation of the greenhouse effect, which of these three planets cannot have a greenhouse effect at all?
questions.a: Mercury, because it has no atmosphere with gases to trap heat
o: Mercury, because it has no atmosphere with gases to trap heat
Venus, because it is already the hottest planet
Earth, because its temperature is just right
None of them, because all three get their energy from the Sun

questions.q:
Read these statements.
I. On Earth, gases like carbon dioxide trap heat by absorbing the radiation that Earth gives off after it is warmed by the Sun.
II. A plant greenhouse keeps warm in the same way as Earth: gases like carbon dioxide inside it absorb radiation.
III. The greenhouse effect makes Earth too hot for water to stay liquid.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only
o: I only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Venus is the hottest planet in the solar system.
Reason (R): Venus is the planet closest to the Sun.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Define the greenhouse effect on a planet, and name one gas that the chapter says causes it.
questions.a: The greenhouse effect is the trapping of heat by gases in a planet's atmosphere: they absorb the radiation the planet gives off after the Sun warms it, so the heat does not escape. Carbon dioxide is one such gas.
s: Gases in the atmosphere trap heat by absorbing the radiation given off by the warmed planet
Names carbon dioxide

questions.q:
Tanvi notices that a car parked in the sun with all its windows shut becomes very hot inside.
(a) Is this more like a plant greenhouse or like the greenhouse effect of a planet?
(b) Give a reason from the chapter for your answer.
questions.a: (a) It is more like a plant greenhouse. (b) The car is a closed space with glass windows, so the air inside warms up and stays in, and the heat does not escape easily. The greenhouse effect of a planet works differently: gases like carbon dioxide absorb the radiation given off by the warmed planet.
s: (a) Like a plant greenhouse
(b) A closed glass space traps the warmed air, unlike gases absorbing radiation on a planet

questions.q:
Table 13.2 gives: Mercury, average temperature 170 °C, no atmosphere; Venus, 450 °C, has an atmosphere; Earth, 15 °C, has an atmosphere. The three planets are listed in order of distance from the Sun, nearest first. Two students each propose a rule.
Rule 1 (Kiran): 'The closer a planet is to the Sun, the hotter it is.'
Rule 2 (Zoya): 'A planet with an atmosphere is always hotter than a planet without one.'
(a) Test Rule 1 on the table: which pair of planets breaks it, and how?
(b) Test Rule 2 on the table: which pair of planets breaks it, and how?
(c) Neither rule fits every row. Using the chapter, write one corrected rule that fits all three planets.
questions.a: (a) Mercury and Venus: Venus is farther from the Sun than Mercury, yet it is hotter (450 °C against 170 °C). (b) Mercury and Earth: Earth has an atmosphere, yet it is much colder (15 °C) than Mercury (170 °C), which has none. (c) For example: 'Planets closer to the Sun are generally hotter, but a thick atmosphere of gases like carbon dioxide traps heat (the greenhouse effect) and can make a farther planet, like Venus, hotter than a closer one.'
s: (a) Mercury and Venus: Venus is farther but hotter (450 °C against 170 °C)
(b) Mercury and Earth: Earth has an atmosphere but is colder (15 °C against 170 °C)
(c) Closer planets are generally hotter, but a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere trapping heat can make a farther planet hotter

questions.q: Dev says: 'Mars and Jupiter are next to each other in the order of planets from the Sun, so they must be the same kind of planet: both small and rocky.' Check his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. In order of increasing distance from the Sun, the planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Mars is the fourth planet and the last of the four relatively small, rocky planets. Jupiter is the fifth planet and the first of the four large planets mostly made of gases. So the line between the two kinds of planets falls exactly between Mars and Jupiter; being neighbours does not make them the same kind.
s: States that the claim is wrong
Mars, the fourth planet, is one of the small rocky planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars)
Jupiter, the fifth, is the first of the large gas planets, so the rocky/gas divide falls between Mars and Jupiter

questions.q:
For Science Day, a Class 8 group in Hyderabad builds a model of the solar system along a school corridor. The Sun is a yellow disc on the end wall, and the eight planets hang from the ceiling in their order from the Sun. Rocky planets are made as clay balls and planets made mostly of gases as balloons. The model Earth is a clay ball of radius 20 cm, and the group uses Table 13.2 to size Venus.
(a) How many clay balls must the group make, and for which planets?
(b) What radius should the clay ball for Venus have?
(c) Which planet hangs just after Mars, and is it a clay ball or a balloon?
(d) Which two planets hang between the Sun and Earth?
questions.a: (a) Four clay balls: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. (b) Venus's radius is 0.95 times Earth's, so 0.95 × 20 = 19 cm. (c) Jupiter, a balloon, since it is a large planet mostly made of gases. (d) Mercury and Venus.
s: (a) Four: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars
(c) Jupiter, a balloon
(d) Mercury and Venus

questions.q: What is the range of distances from the Sun (or another star) over which water remains liquid called?
questions.a: The habitable zone, also called the Goldilocks zone
o: The habitable zone, also called the Goldilocks zone
The ozone layer
The greenhouse zone
The magnetic field

questions.q: Two imaginary planets, M and N, both lie in their star's habitable zone and both have the same average density as Earth. M is about the size of Earth; N is much smaller. Going by the chapter, which planet is more likely to keep an atmosphere?
questions.a: M, because its gravity is strong enough to hold on to the gases, while N's weaker gravity would let them escape into space
o: M, because its gravity is strong enough to hold on to the gases, while N's weaker gravity would let them escape into space
N, because a smaller planet has less air to hold, so it keeps its air more easily
Both equally, because any planet in the habitable zone keeps its atmosphere
Neither can be said, because only a magnetic field, not gravity, holds a planet's atmosphere

questions.q: In an illustrative drawing, the air above a patch of ground on Earth is shown as 300 dots. Using what the chapter says about the atmosphere of Mars compared with Earth's, how many dots should be drawn above the same patch of ground on Mars?
questions.a: 3 dots
o: 3 dots
30 dots
200 dots
30,000 dots

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I: 1. Cosmic rays, 2. Solar wind, 3. Ultraviolet (UV) rays from the Sun, 4. Movement of molten iron in Earth's core
Column II: A. Believed to be the origin of Earth's magnetic field, B. High-energy particles that come from the Sun, C. High-energy particles that come from far across the universe, D. Blocked by the ozone layer

Assertion (A): The atmosphere on Mars is 100 times thinner than the atmosphere on Earth.
Reason (R): Mars lies at the edge of the Sun's habitable zone.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: True or false? 'Cosmic rays and the solar wind can reduce the ozone layer.' Give a reason.
questions.a: True. These tiny high-energy particles from space can damage the atmosphere and reduce the ozone layer, which lets in more harmful UV rays.
s: States True
Reason: these high-energy particles damage the atmosphere and reduce the ozone layer, letting in more UV rays

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) Why is Earth called the Blue Planet?
(b) What do scientists think Mars may have had in the past?
(c) Some of the oxygen in our atmosphere changes into another form that makes a protective layer. Name this form, and say what the layer blocks.
questions.a: (a) Most of Earth's surface is covered with water, so it looks blue from space. (b) Liquid water, maybe even some lakes, and conditions that could support simple life forms. (c) Ozone; the ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays from the Sun that can damage living cells.
s: (a) Most of the surface is covered with water, so Earth looks blue from space
(b) Liquid water (maybe lakes) that could support simple life
(c) Ozone, which blocks harmful UV rays

questions.q: Ananya writes in her notebook: 'Mars lies in the Sun's habitable zone and rovers have explored it, so scientists have proved that life exists on Mars.' Check her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: The conclusion is wrong. Mars lies only at the edge of the Sun's habitable zone. Spacecraft have been sent and rovers have explored its surface, but no proof of life has been found yet. Scientists only think that Mars may once have had liquid water and conditions that could support simple life, and science stays open to new clues.
s: States that the conclusion (that life on Mars has been proved) is wrong
Mars is only at the edge of the habitable zone
No proof of life has been found; scientists only think it may once have had liquid water

questions.q:
Astronomers (in an illustrative example) find three rocky planets going round a Sun-like star. Each is about Earth's size and has a similar thin atmosphere, and they are listed in order of distance from the star, nearest first. Their average temperatures are: Planet P, 150 °C; Planet Q, 20 °C; Planet R, -60 °C. Take it that water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C.
(a) In which form would most of the water be on each planet?
(b) On which planet can water stay liquid? Using the chapter's meaning of the term, which planet lies in the star's habitable zone?
(c) Some microbes might survive on Planet R. What does the chapter say that supports this?
(d) Which planet could best support plants and animals? Explain why the other two could not, even if microbes lived on R.
questions.a: (a) P: the water would have evaporated, since 150 °C is above 100 °C; Q: liquid, since 20 °C lies between 0 °C and 100 °C; R: frozen as ice, since -60 °C is below 0 °C. (b) Water can stay liquid only on Q. The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star over which water remains liquid, so Q lies in it; P, nearer the star, is too hot and R, farther away, is too cold. (c) The chapter says some microbes, like certain bacteria, can survive in frozen environments. (d) Q. Liquid water is essential for life to evolve and for most life forms, especially plants and animals, to grow and thrive. On P it is too hot and the water evaporates; on R it is too cold and the water freezes, so plants and animals could not grow and thrive there.
s: (a) P: evaporated (above 100 °C); Q: liquid; R: frozen (below 0 °C)
(b) Q: only there water stays liquid, and the habitable zone is the range of distances where water stays liquid
(c) Some microbes, like certain bacteria, can survive in frozen environments
(d) Q: liquid water is essential for plants and animals; P too hot (water evaporates), R too cold (water freezes)

questions.q:
For each situation, name the feature of Earth that the chapter says is responsible.
(a) Most of the harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun do not reach living cells on the ground.
(b) A freely suspended magnet always settles in a fixed direction.
(c) The air we breathe does not escape into space.
(d) Most places on Earth do not swing between extreme summers and extreme winters during the year.
(e) Earth is neither so close to the Sun that all its water would evaporate, nor so far away that all of it would freeze.
questions.a: (a) The ozone layer in the atmosphere. (b) Earth's magnetic field: Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet. (c) Earth's right size: its gravity is strong enough to hold on to the gases of the atmosphere. (d) Earth's nearly circular orbit, which keeps the sunlight and heat it receives nearly steady through the year. (e) Earth's position: it is at just the right distance from the Sun, in the habitable zone, where water stays liquid.
s: (a) The ozone layer
(b) Earth's magnetic field (Earth behaves like a giant magnet)
(c) Earth's right size, whose gravity holds the atmosphere
(d) Earth's nearly circular orbit
(e) Earth's position: the right distance from the Sun, in the habitable zone

questions.q: All of Earth's water, in ponds, lakes, rivers, springs, seas, oceans and groundwater, together forms which Earth system?
questions.a: The hydrosphere
o: The hydrosphere
The atmosphere
The geosphere
The biosphere

questions.q: Which of these examples shows the atmosphere and the hydrosphere affecting each other?
questions.a: Water vapour in the air forms clouds that bring rain and refill lakes and rivers
o: Water vapour in the air forms clouds that bring rain and refill lakes and rivers
Water in the soil carries nutrients up to the leaves of a plant
Plants and animals take oxygen from the air for respiration
Tiny plankton and giant whales live in the oceans, lakes and rivers

questions.q:
Read these statements.
I. Geodiversity is the variety of animals and plants found in a place.
II. The biosphere includes land, water and air, where life interacts with its surroundings.
III. Water carries nutrients from the soil to the leaves of plants.
Which of these statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Without an atmosphere, Earth would lose heat to space and become too cold.
Reason (R): The atmosphere contains oxygen, which humans, animals and plants use for respiration.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: What is the geosphere? Name one mineral or metal that the chapter says it gives us.
questions.a: The geosphere is the solid part of the Earth, made of rocks, soils and minerals. It gives us, for example, salt, coal, oil, iron or copper.
s: The solid part of Earth: rocks, soils and minerals
Names one of salt, coal, oil, iron or copper

questions.q: State two ways in which water helps the body of an animal, as given in the chapter.
questions.a: Any two of these: it regulates body temperature, it aids digestion, and it ensures hydration.
s: First role: regulates body temperature, aids digestion or ensures hydration
A second, different role from the same list

questions.q:
Answer briefly.
(a) What does the biosphere consist of?
(b) What do decomposers do?
(c) What does geodiversity help to create?
questions.a: (a) All living beings together with the places where they live, that is land, water and air. (b) They break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. (c) Unique habitats where different types of life can thrive.
s: (a) All living beings and the places where they live (land, water, air)
(b) Break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil
(c) Unique habitats for different types of life

questions.q: Kabir says: 'Plants give out oxygen in sunlight, so they never need to take in oxygen themselves.' Which part of his claim is right and which part is wrong? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is partly right. The first part is right: in the presence of sunlight, plants take carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil to make food by photosynthesis, and oxygen is released. The second part is wrong: the chapter says the oxygen in the atmosphere is used for respiration by humans, animals and plants, so plants do need to take in oxygen.
s: First part right: in sunlight, plants make food by photosynthesis and release oxygen
Second part wrong: plants, like humans and animals, use oxygen from the air for respiration
Verdict: partly right; the first part is true but the conclusion that plants never need oxygen is wrong

questions.q:
Ramesh, a farmer near Gaya in Bihar, grows wheat on two equal plots with the same kind of soil. Into Plot A he digs compost made from crop remains, dry leaves and cow dung that has rotted in a pit for some months. To Plot B he adds nothing. At harvest (illustrative figures), Plot A gives 30 quintals of wheat and Plot B gives 24 quintals. Making compost for one more plot of this size would cost him about as much as 2 quintals of wheat.
(a) To which Earth system does the soil of the plots belong?
(b) By what percentage is Plot A's harvest greater than Plot B's?
(c) Using the chapter, explain how the compost made Plot A's soil richer, and name the living things that did this work.
(d) Should Ramesh make compost for Plot B next season too? Decide using the figures, taking it that Plot B would then give the same harvest as Plot A.
questions.a: (a) The geosphere. (b) (30 - 24) / 24 x 100 = 25 per cent. (c) Decomposers broke down the dead matter in the compost (the remains of plants and animals) and returned nutrients to the soil, so Plot A's soil had more of the nutrients plants need to grow. (d) Yes. Composting Plot B would add 30 - 24 = 6 quintals of wheat and cost about 2 quintals, so he would gain about 4 quintals more each season.
s: (a) Geosphere
(b) 6 / 24 x 100 = 25 per cent
(c) Decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil
(d) Yes: extra 6 quintals against a cost of 2 quintals, a net gain of about 4 quintals

questions.q:
Rice grows in a field in the Godavari delta of Andhra Pradesh. One year, the winds bring very little water vapour over the delta, and hardly any clouds form all season. Trace this one change through Earth's systems.
(a) In which Earth system does the change start, and what does water vapour in the air normally do?
(b) How would the hydrosphere around the field be affected?
(c) The rice plant takes water from the soil. Name two jobs this water does for the plant that would now suffer.
(d) If the rice plants make less food by photosynthesis, how would this affect the air and the animals that depend on the plants?
(e) What does this chain of effects show about how Earth sustains life?
questions.a: (a) In the atmosphere; water vapour in the air normally forms clouds and brings rain. (b) With little rain, the rivers, lakes and underground water would not be refilled, so less water would reach the field. (c) Water carries nutrients from the soil to the leaves, and it is used, with carbon dioxide from the air, to make food by photosynthesis. (d) The plants would take in less carbon dioxide and release less oxygen, which living things need for respiration, and animals that eat the plants would have less food. (e) Earth is a vast living system in which air, water, land and living things support and affect one another, so a change in one part affects the others; life survives because everything works together in balance.
s: (a) Atmosphere; water vapour forms clouds and brings rain
(b) Rivers, lakes and underground water are not refilled
(c) Water carries nutrients from soil to leaves and is used in photosynthesis
(d) Less carbon dioxide taken in and less oxygen released; less food for animals that eat plants
(e) Earth's systems support and affect one another, so a change in one part affects the others

questions.q: In sexual reproduction, each parent makes specialised reproductive cells that carry only half of the parent's genetic material. What are these cells called?

questions.a: Both in the water, outside the female's body
o: Both in the water, outside the female's body
Fertilisation inside the female's body, development in the water
Both inside the female's body

questions.q:
Match each gamete (Column I) with its description (Column II).
Column I: 1. Pollen grain, 2. Ovule, 3. Sperm, 4. Egg
Column II: A. Female gamete of a flowering plant, B. Male gamete of an animal, C. Male gamete of a flowering plant, D. Female gamete of an animal

Reason (R): Growing a plant from a cutting is vegetative propagation, a kind of asexual reproduction in which a single parent produces the new individual.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

Assertion (A): Bacteria can reproduce only asexually.
Reason (R): Bacteria divide into two identical individuals.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: True or false? 'In sexual reproduction, each offspring is an exact copy of one of its two parents.' Give a reason or write the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. In sexual reproduction, instructions from two parents combine, half from each, so the offspring shares some traits with both parents but is not exactly like either of them.
s: States False
Corrects it: instructions from both parents mix, so the offspring resembles but is not identical to either parent

questions.q:
(a) What is pollination?
(b) In a flower, what is formed when the male and female gametes combine at fertilisation, and what does it become?
questions.a: (a) Pollination is the carrying of pollen to another flower by wind, insects or animals. (b) A zygote is formed, and it becomes the seed.
s: (a) Pollen carried to another flower by wind, insects or animals
(b) A zygote, which becomes the seed

questions.q:
In an illustrative model, every body cell of a mango tree carries 40 'instruction cards'. Pollen from Tree X reaches a flower of Tree Y, and a seed forms. Two students predict how many cards the seed's first cell (the zygote) will carry.
Asha: 'The pollen and the ovule each carry all 40 cards, so the zygote gets 80.'
Kabir: 'The pollen and the ovule each carry 20 cards, so the zygote gets 40.'
(a) If Asha were right, the seedling's cells would carry 80 cards and each of its gametes 80 too. Following her idea, with both parents always from the same generation, how many cards would the cells of the next generation carry, and of the generation after that?
(b) Whose prediction agrees with the chapter? Give the chapter's reason.
(c) In Kabir's model the seedling has 40 cards, just like each parent tree. Explain why it will still not be an exact copy of Tree Y.
questions.a: (a) 160 and then 320: the number would double in every generation (80 + 80 = 160, then 160 + 160 = 320). (b) Kabir's. The chapter says each parent makes gametes that carry only half of the parent's genetic material, so when the male and female gametes join, the new cell gets a complete set, half from each parent, and the instructions do not keep doubling every generation. (c) Its 40 cards are a mix: 20 came from Tree X through the pollen and 20 from Tree Y through the ovule, and each gamete carries a different set of instructions, so the seedling resembles Tree Y but is not identical to it.
s: (a) 160, then 320: Asha's idea doubles the cards every generation
(b) Kabir's: gametes carry only half the parent's genetic material, so the zygote gets a complete set, half from each parent, with no doubling
(c) Its cards are a mix, 20 from Tree X (pollen) and 20 from Tree Y (ovule), so it is not an exact copy of Tree Y

questions.q:
A jamun tree (Tree A) grows in a park in Lucknow. In spring, insects carry pollen to its flowers from another jamun tree (Tree B) across the road. In summer, langurs eat Tree A's ripe fruits and drop the seeds in a garden far away. After the monsoon rains, two jamun seedlings come up there.
(a) Which tree supplied the male gametes, and which supplied the female gametes, for these seeds?
(b) Using (a), explain why the seedlings may not be exactly like Tree A.
(c) Will the two seedlings be exactly like each other? Explain.
(d) How did the seedlings come to grow far from Tree A, and what did each seed use to grow its first roots and shoots?
questions.a: (a) Tree B supplied the male gametes, in its pollen grains; Tree A supplied the female gametes, its ovules. (b) At fertilisation, instructions from the two parents, Tree A and Tree B, combined in the zygote that became the seed, so a seedling is not exactly like either parent. (c) No. Each gamete carries a different set of instructions, and these mix in a different way each time, so the two seedlings will differ from each other, just as brothers and sisters do. (d) The langurs ate the fruits and dropped the seeds far from the parent tree, a helpful way for plants to spread; when the seeds got water in the rains, they used their stored nutrients to grow roots and shoots.
s: (a) Tree B gave the male gametes (pollen); Tree A gave the female gametes (ovules)
(b) Instructions from two parents combine at fertilisation, so a seedling is not an exact copy of Tree A
(c) No: each gamete carries a different set of instructions that mix differently each time
(d) Langurs ate the fruit and dropped the seeds far away; with water, the seed used stored nutrients

questions.q:
Say whether each of these is asexual or sexual reproduction, and give the reason in a few words.
(a) A Hydra grows a tiny bud on its body, which breaks off and grows into a new Hydra.
(b) A small cut part of an alga regrows into a new alga.
(c) A female fish releases eggs and a male fish releases sperm into the water, where they combine.
(d) The 'eyes' of a sprouted potato, planted in moist soil, grow into new plants.
(e) Pollen from one mustard flower reaches another mustard flower, and seeds form.
questions.a: (a) Asexual: a single parent; its bud grows into a new individual. (b) Asexual: a single parent regrows from a cut part. (c) Sexual: male and female gametes (sperm and eggs) from two parents combine. (d) Asexual: vegetative propagation from one parent plant. (e) Sexual: pollen (male gamete) and ovule (female gamete) combine at fertilisation to form seeds.
s: (a) Asexual: one parent; the bud grows into a new Hydra
(b) Asexual: one parent regrows from a cut part
(c) Sexual: sperm and eggs from two parents combine
(d) Asexual: vegetative propagation from one parent
(e) Sexual: male and female gametes combine to form seeds

questions.q:
Two farmers near Nashik grow wheat in neighbouring fields. Farmer A uses as much fertiliser as his crop needs. Farmer B uses three times as much, hoping for a much bigger harvest.
(a) Whose field is more likely to suffer soil pollution, and which part of the triple planetary crisis is this?
(b) Using the chapter, explain why Farmer B's plan may give him a smaller harvest instead.
questions.a: (a) Farmer B's field; this is pollution (soil pollution), one of the three parts of the triple planetary crisis. (b) The chapter says excess fertilisers pollute the soil and reduce crop yield, so using far more than the crop needs can lower his harvest instead of raising it.
s: (a) Farmer B; pollution (soil pollution)
(b) Excess fertilisers pollute the soil and reduce crop yield, so the harvest may fall

(b) Sea levels and coastal cities

(b) Sea levels rise and coastal cities could flood
(c) Many plants and animals disappear

questions.q:
Every school day, 30 children from a housing colony in Nagpur are driven to school in 30 separate cars, which together burn 15 litres of petrol (illustrative figures). The colony can fund only one plan this year. Plan A: one school bus for all 30 children, burning 5 litres of fuel a day. Plan B: a 'walking group' for the 10 children who live close to the school, while the other 20 still come by car. Take every litre of fuel as releasing about the same amount of greenhouse gas.
(a) Name the two parts of the triple planetary crisis that the burning of fuel in these cars adds to.
(b) How many litres of petrol a day would Plan B still burn, if every car burns the same amount?
(c) By how many litres a day would each plan cut the fuel burnt?
(d) Which plan should the colony choose to cut its greenhouse gases most? Justify using your answers and the chapter's advice.
questions.a: (a) Climate change (burning fuel releases greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, which trap heat and cause global warming) and pollution (air pollution from vehicles). (b) Each car burns 15 / 30 = 0.5 litres, so 20 cars burn 20 x 0.5 = 10 litres. (c) Plan A: 15 - 5 = 10 litres; Plan B: 15 - 10 = 5 litres. (d) Plan A, because it cuts twice as much fuel (10 litres against 5 litres a day), so it releases less greenhouse gas and causes less air pollution; this follows the chapter's advice to choose environmentally friendly ways to travel. Plan B also helps, but it cuts only half as much.
s: (a) Climate change and pollution
(b) 15 / 30 = 0.5 litres per car; 20 x 0.5 = 10 litres
(c) Plan A cuts 10 litres; Plan B cuts 5 litres
(d) Plan A, since it cuts twice as much fuel (10 against 5 litres), in line with environmentally friendly travel

questions.q:
A small town beside a river in Punjab dumps factory waste and plastic into the river, and the farmers around it use far more fertiliser than their crops need. Many families in the town eat fish from the river and vegetables from these farms, though they drink only filtered water.
(a) Name the Earth system that the factory waste harms first, and say what the chapter says such waste does to it.
(b) Name the Earth system that the extra fertiliser harms first, and say what this does to the farmers' crops.
(c) Trace one path by which harmful substances from the river or the fields could still reach a family that drinks only filtered water.
(d) Use (a) to (c) to explain why the chapter says damage to one Earth system can affect the others.
(e) Name the remedy the chapter gives for each of the two problems.
questions.a: (a) The hydrosphere (the river); factory and plastic waste harm aquatic life and make the water unsafe. (b) The geosphere (the soil); excess fertiliser pollutes the soil and reduces the crop yield. (c) For example, harmful substances from the polluted soil get into the vegetables grown there, and spread through the food chain to the family who eat them (or they pass from the river into the fish that the family eats). (d) The damage starts in the water and the soil but passes into living things, the biosphere, including people, because all Earth systems are connected. (e) Better waste management for the waste dumped in the river, and sustainable farming practices for the excess fertiliser.
s: (a) Hydrosphere; the waste harms aquatic life and makes water unsafe
(b) Geosphere; excess fertiliser pollutes the soil and reduces crop yield
(c) Harmful substances pass from soil (or water) into crops (or fish) and spread through the food chain to people
(d) Damage in water and soil passes into living things (biosphere), because the Earth systems are connected
(e) Better waste management (river) and sustainable farming practices (fields)
